utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Niemann?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honour. Your Honour, before I call the next witness, there are two photographs taken in relation to the witness Hodzic on Friday when it was shown on the screen here with the video camera. These have now been produced and I tender them. Might they be marked 313A and 313B? They were taken off the video.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Is there any objection from the Defence?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: No, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Exhibits 313A and 313B will be admitted. We orally granted the motion of the Prosecutor for protective measures for witness S ----

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: --- who we will be hearing from next. There was no objection on the part of Defence so we will proceed with witness S with image distortion otherwise we will be in closed -- open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Open session, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Open session. So the usher will have to lower the shades for the witness to come in, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I call witness S, your Honour. WITNESS S, called.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: There will be no recording, of course, when witness S comes in. Sir, would you please take the oath that has been handed to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Fine. Thank you. You may be seated.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Could I ask the usher to show this piece of paper to the Defence and then to give it to the witness, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Witness, would you please look at the piece of paper you now see and tell me if your name appears on that paper?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Thank you. Sir, were you born on 24th March 1940?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Where were you born?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In Kozarac, settlement Mutnik, and I grew up in Krkici at the crossroads of Kozarac/Banja Luka/Prijedor road.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did you go to primary school, do your primary school, in Kozarac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Primary school I completed in Kozarac, in the old school building. To clarify that, in the old school building in Kozarac.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did you attend your secondary school also in Kozarac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The high school, or that was the training as a baker, I completed with my father Kulasic also at the crossroads across from the school in Kozarac.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Your father was the baker in Kozarac and did you follow him as being the baker of Kozarac as well?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I finished the school for baker and my father was a baker and up until this war he kept a bakery, and it was inherited by Meho, my younger brother, and most recently it was his bakery in Kozarac and my father was retired.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: In what part of Kozarac was the bakery that your family operated and ran?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My family kept the bakery somewhere around 50 metres from the crossroads of the old road, Prijedor/Banja Luka, and about 500 metres from the new asphalt towards Mrakovica going from the new asphalt towards the national park, Kozara, Mrakovica, about 500 metres away to the old intersection. The bakery was across the street from the new primary school in Kozarac and in that bakery most recently there was (redacted) Mehmed, baker. That is my brother, my father's son.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Perhaps you should not mention names other than the first names perhaps. Would you tell me when you did your military service?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. My military service, I served from 18 August '58 to the 1st August 1960.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did you do that, firstly, in Sarajevo and then in Montenegro?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: First, I was in Sarajevo, in Butile, in the military bakery, and then I was transferred to Niksic in Montenegro.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Are you by religion a Muslim?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Both my father and mother are Muslims, so I am a Muslim too and that is why I am guilty.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: At the beginning of 1992 had you retired?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At the beginning of 1992 I retired as a -- but I worked in the biscuit factory and then before that I was handicapped and then I was on disability, and then after 1992 I was fully retired.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did you live about one and a half kilometres down the old Prijedor road from the centre of the town of Kozarac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I lived 1.5 kilometres away from -- kilometre towards Prijedor on the old asphalt road.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Were you in Kozarac on the day it was attacked on 24th May 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In my own house I found myself there on the day of the attack and I was taken prisoner in that same house.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did you stay in the house because of the state of your health?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I stayed in the house because of my health conditions, and in the other shelters where I had information that I could go, there were a lot of children and I was -- and I have asthma as my condition.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did one of your sons stay with you in your house?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My older son Adem stayed with me because of my health. He was under my staircase in my own house.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: At one point did a tank come up to your house and put the gun turret through the window of the house?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At one point we heard, that is, my son and I, that something was approaching that looked like a tank. We could not see it until the barrel came through and then a shot, a shell, and I heard that something was broken, and then when I -- later when I got out, I saw that it went over my son's car, Yugo, that it went over it and that it broke through the window and that it -- as if people were acting out. I do not know why they did it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Your Honour, at this stage might I request a redaction at 10.17, page 4, line 5? Your Honour, it is the word which -----

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Yes, I see it. Is there any objection? It would be the sixth word and then -----

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: It is 5 and 6, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Just the name? Do you want anything else? The last word or -- OK. It is up to you to tell me and then I will get a response.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Your Honour, we would be happy if the sixth word stayed in but the fifth word, even though it is not spelt correctly here in the transcript, when it is corrected it would not be a problem ----

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: OK.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: --- so if the fifth word could go and the sixth word could stay.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Very good. Any objection?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: That will be granted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: Mr. Niemann, I do not know if the tank incident is of any significance, but if it is I do not think it is at all clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: It is not of great significance, your Honour. I think I will move on. [To the witness]: Were you then taken as prisoner? Were you then captured?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The tank was in front of the house and it fired a shell, two unknown young men came and ran up and on the way back, because I responded, they captured me and they asked for the arms and I gave them a pistol I had and they took myself and my son out of the house.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did they take your son at that stage or just you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My son was taken away somewhere, I do not know where, in what direction, but only I stayed in front of the house and from across the road.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Were you then loaded on to a bus?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: After that there was a lot of mistreatment on the part of this person from the tank who got out and mistreated me. For a while he walked me up and down the asphalt, and told me that somebody from his family had died, that his uncle or something, that I would be his uncle, and that I would look like him if I was, I was to be beheaded, and that was a lot of chicanery and it went on for about half an hour. Then the young man who had taken my pistol away from me came back and grabbed me by the scruff of my neck and pushed me into the bus, and I came in. I was afraid of him, so I sort of crouched. Then he came looking for me and he found a person who looked like me. He slapped him twice and somebody said, "No, that is not the one" and then he got the other slap and the bus started, and I considered myself lucky to have been on that bus, and I went to Prijedor. If I need to go on, I will go on.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: No. When you got on the bus, the person who was driving the tank, the man that abused you, came on the bus looking for you but could not find you. He mistook you for somebody else, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: He then got off the bus and the bus went off to Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: When you went to Prijedor you went to a place near the SUP?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The bus stopped between the SUP and the municipality building, and the men were taken off the bus. We went through the cordon of the military. I do not know if they were the police or the military because they were wearing the uniforms of the reserve military. So we went through this cordon. Everybody got something, either with a rifle butt or a baton, until we went into the SUP and went into the back building. So it was, it was the building in the back, in the courtyard, in the back.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: When you say "everybody got something", you mean everybody got hit?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. That is what I meant.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: When you finally had gone through the cordon, did you then empty everything out of your pockets on to the ground?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When we went past through the cordon, then we went through into the cordon and we had to put up our hands up like this and then they said, "Take the right arm and empty everything from the right pocket, and then the same from, take down the left hand and empty the left pockets". After that we could not see what was going on behind us because whoever budged, even a millimetre, they would be beaten. During that I heard the conversation and a man walked in from somewhere, I do not know who he was, but he was whimpering. Then we were told to pick up everything that was there, either the wallets or the personal identity card, whatever we had thrown out of our pockets and whatever they wanted they had picked up as evidence or something. In that moment nothing was taken away from me, neither my personal ID card or my military veteran book, nothing, not even money at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: After all this had happened and sometime later, were you loaded back on to the bus or the mini van and were you taken to the Keraterm camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: After all that a van arrived, I think it was Zastava make, and we were loaded in the back, and we started in what to me was then an unknown direction. Then we came to a railroad overpass. I had a sense that that was what was happening and so I thought that we were going towards Banja Luka. After that short time, I found myself in front of Keraterm and the van turned around and we got off into that building, and I called this “boxes”. Those were rooms in Keraterm where they were drying, I do not know what they had, tiles or something. So we called them box 1, box 2, box 3, box 4. So, in Keraterm there were those boxes. That is how I was calling them and also the ones who were with me. I was in box 3.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: These boxes were part of the process of making the tiles, were they?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: They were large enough to hold quite a number of people?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were very large, but all that number of people who were there at that point was not really sufficient, that is, it was so crowded one could not sit down. If one did sit down, you could not stand up, that is, everybody had to move to one side and pack into one side so that somebody could make a move. We were totally packed there, and they were pushing us in so that they could close the door. The door was metal and it was closed, then pushing us in. But they were very large, I mean, those boxes. They were not small.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Then were people taken out in groups and interrogated?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On 26th, when I was taken out, a group of people were taken out for interrogation, but not all were taken for interrogation. They were taken out of these boxes. They were people of elder generation who went for interrogation, either they first or what, I was not really abreast of what was happening, but there were not, at any rate, any young people who went for interrogation. Whether anybody went before that, I could not see. But young people were passing by, one by one, next to my box and where did they go, whether for interrogation or something else, I could not see at the time. The examination was for us elderly. There were 52, I think, 50 people were interrogated during that first go in Keraterm -- not there, they would call you out and then take you for interrogation.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: At your interrogation did you produce your military booklet which had a special stamp on it and did they consider that you had been disabled or were disabled?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At the exit from the building for interrogation, there could go a man who was 60 or, perhaps, 65 and invalids who were -- who could not move, and I had this booklet showing that I was a wartime military invalid. I showed them my booklet and that guard told me, excuse me, that that man who had captured me was nuts, crazier than I was, and told me "Go out". Perhaps this young man really thought that I was a wartime invalid because I had this acronym RMI which, in our language, would mean a wartime military invalid, but it was not that. I was invalided when I served the army, not in wartime. So, of course, all the invalids, they were financed from one and the same till. Our fringe benefits were paid out from one and the same place, both for us who were wartime invalids and those who were invalided in peace time but in the army. Whether he knew what that booklet was, whether he did not, whether he had ever seen it before or not, I do not know, but that is how I got out. That is how I was fortunate enough to get out and very many of my colleagues were not as fortunate and did not get out.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: But were you then later interrogated, a few hours later, two hours later?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: On this occasion did they beat you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not the first time, the second time.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is another question.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: The second time I am asking you about. On the second occasion were you beaten?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: About the second interrogation, the second interrogation I was called. I do not know who was on the interrogation commission, but there were several pictures, there were several photographs they had showing my family house. On the ground floor was a shop and a coffee bar, and I could notice a soldier coming out wearing a uniform. I could not see it because it was taken from a great distance. I could not recognise the soldier but I recognised my house. I recognised the shop and I saw that it was a soldier or something, and the first question was, how much money had I donated to the Ustasha. The second question, how much bread had I given to the Ustasha. The third question, at least while I was still conscious and the beating had started because they were beating me then, but the third question I really was aware of was, how long was I going to feed the extremists? After that I knew nothing because then my jaw was broken. I wore prosthesis. All this was broken. On the prosthesis there is a steel wire and all the teeth fell out and the wire, I guess, stretched or changed, so it pricked me. I lost consciousness. I was taken out. What happened next, whether they went on beating me, how much they beat me, I simply do not know. I woke up on the lower floor next to a wash basin. Two soldiers were holding me there and one was pouring water on my neck and that is when I regain consciousness.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Do you know the accused in these proceedings, Dusko Tadic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Dusko Tadic, his family, I have known since, that is, his father I have known since '47, '48, he was my next door neighbour until the restaurant was built, and a man called Salih Hamic built a house between our two houses. So, my father's house and Ostoja Tadic's house, the late Ostoja Tadic's, were one next to the other practically. There was nothing between them. It was an empty space there. Nothing existed there for a long time, so that we were next door neighbours, that is, our fathers, my father and Mr. Ostoja, Dule's father, were neighbours. So Mr. Ostoja was my first neighbour until Salih Hamic built his house in between.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: During the time that you lived in Kozarac leading up to the war in 1992, did you often see Dule Tadic around the town of Kozarac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Dule, Dusan Tadic, Dule, I saw him often because he had some contacts with my elder son who kept a shop, his own, in my house and his brother's, Mirsad's. So he had a shop and they had some contact, I do not know whether it was a business or what before the war. Right before the war I saw him on the pavement not far from his house, about 100 metres, next to a grill or restaurant, a small grill place, where one could eat, perhaps have a juice or a beer. It was called "Mega". We were passing. He was coming up Kozarac and I was going down Kozarac. I was on the right and he was on the left-hand side. As the houses were, he was going up Kozarac. That was the last time I saw him before the war break out.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Do you refer to the accused as "Dule" Tadic, "Dusan" Tadic or "Dusko" Tadic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I know Dusan as "Dusan", Ostoja Tadic's Dusan, and the nickname was given to him by his colleagues and there is a pet name or something, but I heard him being called "Dule" Tadic, and I always address people in their right name, regardless of whether anyone had a nickname or not. Nicknames are quite a sinful thing sometimes and they can be offensive so I did not want -- I never wanted to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did you know Dusan Tadic's brothers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mladen and Stojan very well, I knew Ljubo less.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Do you know whether or not Dusan Tadic was involved in sporting activities when he was living in Kozarac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mr. Tadic, Mr. Tadic was active in karate. I could see that before he had his coffee bar in his yard behind his own house he had the equipment, karate equipment, and he played with that. I even heard -- I did not see that -- that he had formed a club and that he trained those younger boys, like a karate club or something, and that that was a room or something. I did not see that, but I have heard from some of his relatively close friends that he was a karateist and I saw him in that uniform, in a white, what shall I put it, a white karate uniform behind his house in their yard. Whether he was practising there, training or running up and down, but I saw him practising that. That was a long time ago, 10 years ago or five, six or 10 years ago, rather.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Witness, when you were in the Keraterm camp, did you see Dusan Tadic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Keraterm?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: While I was at the camp, then when I went out for the first examination, I saw Dule Tadic at Keraterm gate next to that, to that small house at the entrance into Keraterm next to that gate where trucks -- next to the scales where trucks are weighed and things, and next to that was a structure, a glass one, from which one could judge how heavy was the freight, the commodity that was weighed there, and he was next to that at the gate in Keraterm. I was some 30 metres away from Mr. Tadic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Do you remember what date this was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That was on 26th May '92.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What time of the day was it, do you recall?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It must have been morning, but more specifically, I do not know if it is very important or not, I could not ascertain that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Where were you when you first saw him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was with several people down Keraterm towards the asphalt road, Prijedor/Banja Luka, somewhere from those scales, about 30 metres away.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did you have a good, unobstructed view of him when you saw him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I could see the gentleman very well, because, let me tell you, it scared me out of my wits. Why do I say that? I felt when I saw a neighbour wearing a uniform, I knew Dule, that is, his family, and I was afraid. Fear seized me because many people who met at that time, I, let me tell you, avoided contact with anyone I had known because they also had known me. They knew me quite well and I avoided contact, and there were also other reasons why I feared that man.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: The uniform that he wore, did you recognise that uniform?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The upper, at the top part was a police uniform, and he had a single colour trousers, and he had something up here behind the lapel, behind the collar. Whether it was a beret or something else, I do not know. It looked like a cap, but it also could have been some insignia. It looked rather stiff. It was that wide and it was in his collar.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: So you think he may have had his hat tucked into the lapel of his coat?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, you know how you have this thing on shirts, and I thought it was a cap, but those soldiers, rather, soldiers, soldiers that I used to see, would wear it there, and also around the sleeve some people had bands, white or blue or red, that I used to see before. So that could also have been some marking, but I still think it was a cap.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: On this occasion when you saw him, did he have a beard or was he clean shaven?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was shaven. He did not have a beard, but whether he was clean shaven or not, do not really ask me that. 30 metres away one can recognise an individual, but to see a beard, no, I am not really sure whether he shaved that day, the day before or two days before or a couple of hours before. I could not say that. But a person I know, and of a slightly dark complexion, when they are some way away that you cannot really recognise whether they are so dark, whether it was simply that the person had not shaved, whether it was just stubble or whether he was really shaven, one could not tell.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: When you knew and saw Dule Tadic in around the town of Kozarac before the war, did you know him as a person who wore a beard or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The gentleman had a beard, but not for long periods of time. Sometime he had a beard -- I did meet him with a beard -- but more often did I see him without a beard.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: When was the next time you saw him in the Keraterm camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The next time I saw him in the Keraterm camp when I went for my second examination. At that time he had his foot on a car -- that was a police car -- and then I had time as I was waiting and I heard more time to observe. With him was, believe it or not, because I know the man, I know he is a taxi driver in Prijedor, and until that time I knew only the surname of that person as a taxi driver. He was -- it was Zigic and they called him "Ziga" but I did not know his first name. He was a taxi driver in Prijedor and his name was Zigic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: This is who ----

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Other particulars, I do not know.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: --- you saw Tadic with on this second occasion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Do you know what date this was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The 27th, 27th May '92.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Do you know what time of the day it was? Was it morning or afternoon?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Afternoon. It was in the afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: About how far were you from Dusan Tadic on this occasion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On that occasion I could have been some 20 metres away, less than 30, maybe 20 metres, but I passed by those people and then I got to a distance of about 30 metres again where we were waiting for some people to be taken out. Some buses were to enter Keraterm and unload, and other guys were boarding some buses going in an unknown direction, and that is when I looked at Tadic and thinking about my two sons who were in Keraterm and those two were there.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: How far was Tadic away from the buses that were arriving and being loaded and unloaded in Keraterm?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The buses passed not more than five metres from Mr. Tadic, less than five metres, as one came in and one went out.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: From what you were able to observe, was Dusan Tadic doing anything with the people who were getting on or off the buses?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What about the person he was with, did you see what he was doing, Zigic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That person was seen in our camp during my first and during my second interrogation as the boss of the camp -- no, I cannot say boss. I do not know what he was, but the person who could issue orders to one of their policeman to bring out such and such a person by name, whether he was the chief or something or a commanding person of some kind, whether he had a position of some authority, I really cannot say, but he evidently had powers to order and pass on a piece of paper. He was not the one who was calling out. He would bid somebody else to give him this and tell him call out this or that. Whether he was their boss or their superior, whether he was what, I do not really know.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did you see Tadic and Zigic do anything together when they were there on this occasion when you were looking at them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were talking, the two of them, but I could not hear what. I could see they were talking, and I could see their mouths opening and closing, but what they talked about, what kind of a conversation they had, that I could not say. I cannot tell you that I heard something when I heard nothing.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did you see them do anything, Tadic and Zigic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I only saw a conversation and some explanation with hands and what were they explaining to each other, I would not know.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: How was Tadic dressed on this occasion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He had a police uniform, like that day he was dressed the same way, except that I saw him different because one of his feet was on the car and his colleague was standing next to him. I saw him a little way away from the scales, from the weighing station, and he was within the grounds. That was the only difference.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did you notice whether or not he had any arms on him, any weapons?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, no, I did not see.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did you see whether or not on this occasion he had any head wear on his person?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I also saw then he was bare headed, and I also saw something under his collar, but what was that, whether it was a cap or what, I do not know.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did you see Tadic give Zigic anything?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In explaining things by hands, that conversation of theirs, I could not really see that. It was not really a friendly conversation. I could realise there was some kind of altercation between them, but what they were talking about, I do not know. Mr. Tadic was facing in my direction and that taxi driver whose name was Zigic, he was a little bit sideways turned and they were explaining something to each other, but I told you already the last time, I do not know what it was, whether they were explaining something to one another, whether they were looking for something, explaining certain things, what they were doing, I did not hear so I cannot tell you I heard Tadic saying that and that because I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: After your stay in Keraterm camp, did you go to the Trnopolje camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Were you in Trnopolje camp from between 17 to 19 days?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: 18 full days. On the 19th I was discharged. I was given a discharge list. Major Kuruzovic or Kuruzovic or something, I think, gave me this discharge letter allowing me to leave the camp and I still have that document with me.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: During the time that you were in Trnopolje camp, did you see Dusan Tadic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I saw Dusan Tadic in Trnopolje, but let me tell you first, the road Trnopolje, that is, railway station Kozarac, on that segment there is also the primary school in Trnopolje where we were in the camp. On the opposite side from the school was once, there used to be a restaurant. It used to belong when I was younger to Husko Elezovic, but when I came to the camp that building was used as the SDS or Serb Army or something headquarters. I do not know what they call it. But, in any event, that was the headquarters on that other side opposite from the school in Trnopolje.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Is this where the camp Commander and the soldiers used to congregate and stay, at this restaurant that you are describing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is where the camp Commander stayed of Trnopolje camp, Commander Mr. Kuruzovic, and his immediate subordinates. Their soldier could, perhaps, go into that structure for orders or for whatever. On the other side was the surgery, rather, ambulanta, the first aid surgery, and there was the Red Cross where subsequently we had to go to apply and ask for permission to go out, and a pub where the soldiers of the Serb Army go to have a juice or a beer, refreshment, get some refreshment, and proceed. There in front of the school, older people and women and personnel looking for some permit to go out or certificate, that is, only those in need of some kind of a document, could cross the road, otherwise it was prohibited to unofficially walk in front of our camp.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Where were you when you saw Dusan Tadic at Trnopolje camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was in front of the Local Commune building in Trnopolje which is next to the school building, and that was also where the Red Cross was when Mr. Tadic arrived there on the asphalt road from Kozarac. Before him, several minutes ahead of him, maybe 20 minutes ahead of him, from that same direction came some kind of a track vehicle with a machine gun on top of it arrived. Then I found myself there in the vicinity where the road -- six to eight metres from the road and I saw Mr. Tadic in Trnopolje there.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Where was Mr. Tadic? Was he on the road, was he?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The first time when I first -- when I first saw him I saw him on the road. He was going down the road to the entrance of that restaurant, but he was not going in there, but at the gate he saw the officers, he saw those officers, and together with them he got again not among the prisoners but in that part of the perimeter of the camp where not everybody was allowed to be, only those who were coming in who had some requests. There were women there. There were women and children who were taking children along with them so that they would be, sort of, protected more, and that is where Tadic came in and that is where the restaurant was where you could consume alcohol or anything else. That was a club at one point of this Local Commune and then it turned into a restaurant. That is where I saw Tadic when he entered, but I was looking at him -- it was for a while -- until he got in. When he already got into the perimeter, then I saw some people in front of me, some movements, so that I could not see his lower part of the body. I only saw the part up, and down the road I saw him completely. When he was going down the roadway, as he was coming inside, then I could see all, the whole person.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: So at first you saw all of him, then he became mixed with a group of people ----

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: -- who were standing waiting to be issued with documents from the restaurant, and at that stage your view of him was at least partially obstructed so you could only see his head or the top half of his body?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Then later between people I saw the upper part.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did you see him with anyone? Did he appear to be talking to anyone when you saw him on this occasion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mr. Tadic at that time spoke to Mr. Major Kuruzovic and two young men were also there, the escorts, bodyguards or escorts, or they were drivers. Believe me, I do not know, but there were two of them, two good looking, strong young men who were always with Mr. Major. Now, what they were talking, I could not tell you. I was scared because when somebody comes from the direction of Kozarac to Trnopolje, then they were coming for something. That is how we saw it; that he was either going to interrogate somebody or to finish off some business which meant the death penalty.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: The person you saw him with was the Commander of the camp and two police officers or two guards were with the Commander?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Two guards or two bodyguards or two drivers, a driver and an escort, I do not know. One was on the other side of the Major and the other one was on this side. Whether the Major had gone into that restaurant or not, there were always two, on rare occasions three, but always two with this Commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did you see how Dusan Tadic arrived there at Trnopolje on that day?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He came, Tadic, with a car that I saw him in the other day in Keraterm. That was the police car, the blue police squad car, darker like behind the Honourable Judges, the background, like this.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: On this occasion when you saw Dusan Tadic in Trnopolje camp, how was he dressed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mr. Tadic even then had, the top was the multicoloured uniform like a shirt or a blouse. I cannot tell you how it was styled. It was open up here. It was a solid colour, pants, and so he was moving around like some kind of a half civilian or a man who had a top of the camouflage -- of the multi-coloured uniform. I cannot tell you that he had a multi-coloured uniform down -- I do not know. It was not a uniform. It was just a solid coloured pants.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: The multi-coloured uniform top, the multi-coloured top, that he had on, that was the police camouflage uniform, was it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The policeman, the special, some of them wore those special multi-colour uniforms, the regular policemen who were -- that we had had the regular police uniform or the winter uniform, and the special police wore those multi-colour with, I do not know, something like leaves, something that would be like a camouflage. Those people were working as interrogators, as lawyers. Those were the ones who were interrogating me and those had those uniforms, some of them. Then others had completely civilian clothes, the ones of those who interrogated. Whether they were using it because the intellectuals wore them among them, I did not -- I had no knowledge of that. It was summer so it was a light, but it was like a shirt or a blouse like camouflage, and the others wore complete police uniforms, the policemen. They wore complete police uniforms that used to exist in Yugoslavia at the time. This between, among soldiers, soldiers wore SMB uniforms and the reservists wore the SMB with some insignia over here, on the sleeve or up on the epaulette. Now, what this meant to them, the top multi-coloured and the bottom solid, I do not know what it meant to them, I cannot explain this, what that fact meant. One should ask the gentleman or some other people who -- he would ----

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: OK.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: -- he would not know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Would you, please, look around the courtroom and tell me if you see the person that you know and recognise as Dusan Tadic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The young man between the two policemen, that is Mr. Tadic, and he knows me very well. I think that we, as neighbours, know each other very well. Look at me, I am ----

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Can you tell me what colour clothes he has on?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He has a jacket, a multi-coloured tie, a white shirt and then his hair is pushed back. Do not ask me too much. We know each other very well. He knows me and I know him. Just be sure that I did not make a mistake.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Might the record reflect, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Yes, the record will reflect that the witness identified the accused.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Cross-examination, Mr. Kay?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Witness, you described being at Keraterm on 26th May 1992, and on this occasion you told us that you saw Dusko Tadic, is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: This was in the morning. I wonder if you could help us with the time in the morning that that would have been? Early hours of the morning, mid morning or late hours of the morning?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can tell you that this was after 10 o'clock, and what time, that is very difficult, the exact time. At that time my hands were shaking and my eyes were darting around. I was looking for people.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: You at this stage were to be interrogated, is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: When you saw Dusko Tadic that morning in Keraterm camp on 26th May, were you on your way to be interrogated?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: After seeing him I went to the interrogation. To clarify, it was the first interrogation, so that I emphasise the first interrogation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: So at the time of seeing him were you inside the box where you were kept or were you outside the box?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At that time I was outside the box, not far from the gentleman, about 30 metres, I already said that, and I was moving. We were standing, because I was not the only one called out to be interrogated. There were more of us. Five by five we went up the stairs to the top floor of Keraterm, five rooms, everybody separated from one another.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: So you were in a group of five prisoners who that morning and at that time were being taken to be questioned in another part of the building?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: You described him as wearing at least at the top part a police uniform and having single coloured trousers? The top part, the police uniform, can you describe that for me?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can only say that the top part of the police uniform are similar to the camouflage uniform -- the JNA special units used to wear them. To clarify this, the people who had special tasks in the JNA, in the woods, in the grass, outdoors, had those uniforms to be similar to the ground, and for us those were the camouflage uniforms, to us. That is a part of the uniform that looks like the ground where they are supposed to execute their duties. At that time they were wearing those uniforms and we in Keraterm, we called them the special police. If you see such a person with such a uniform, he had a special task. Those people, we paid more attention to those people. If you understand me, if you do not understand, I do not know how to explain in another way. That is my ability to explain to you as a Defence counsel how these uniforms, speaking expertly, because I was in the army, I had a lot of contacts with the army and I was a reserve officer. So from based my own professional experience, that is my explanation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: When you said it is a police uniform, do you mean that the basic colour is one of blue?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The police of Yugoslavia, that is, the Yugoslav police had traditionally -- wore traditionally blue uniforms, but SDS took over the power and they had traditional powers and traditional uniforms and traditional authorities and traditionally wanted to kill us all. That is the tradition.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: But on this occasion that you say you saw him, you are clear that he was not wearing a hat on his head, is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Meaning he did not have a hat on his head?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you. As far as you are aware, there was no beard being worn on his face?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When I saw him he did not have a beard, not a pronounced beard. I do not know what you understand as a beard. We, in Bosnia, when you have hair that you can pull it with your hand, that is a beard, but this is a beard, and to have hair, to have facial hair, is to have on that part of the body.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: When you saw him on this occasion, was your view obstructed in any way?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The first time, I am sorry, the first time?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: The distance he was from you was how far?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was up to 30 metres away from me. The first time I saw him he was up to 30 metres away from me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: On this occasion was he on his own or with anyone?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In Keraterm at the gate there was no single person. There was, to make it clear, a person who was communicating with somebody. There were guards that were security that -- the bird could not pass. I know it is foolish to say that, but that is how it was. They had bunkers, they had machine guns -- that you have photographs, you have pictures, what Keraterm was like and what the security was like.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: The next time you saw him you say was the next day in the afternoon, so that would be 27th May?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, 27th, 27th May in the afternoon I was called out for interrogation for the second time and I also had to wait. Probably maybe the gentleman may remember that. I was called out to interrogation and before me the person who went to interrogation was that, no, Baltic Hamdija, and a salesman of construction supply, Sahib Kahrimanovic. So I was there outside for a while and I had a good view and I could see very well Mr. Tadic and his, I do not know if he was his colleagues or -- the taxi driver, Mr. -- his name was Zigic, the taxi driver from Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: When you say the afternoon, was that early afternoon, mid afternoon or late afternoon? Can you help us with the timing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was between 12.00 and 2.30. After 12.00, we have noon at 12.00, and then between 12.00 and 2.30 is the time period when I could see Mr. Tadic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you. You next tell us that you saw him in Trnopolje and you refer to the building opposite the camp that had been a restaurant but was used as an office for the camp Commander as well as a place where soldiers had drinks and met. If internees in the camp had to see the camp Commander to obtain release documents or any other official papers, is that where they would go?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, the person who was issuing the documents in the Red Cross, there were girls who worked as nurses or the officials of the Local Commune, and they were filling out those documents and in a folder, taking it over for it to be certified. What he wanted to see himself, he would cross over to the Red Cross office and he would verify for himself whether a person was disabled or handicapped or something. Those were exceptional cases when he would come into the camp to verify something and often those check-ups, he would just walk up and down the camp and check something, I do not know what.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: By that you mean Major Kuruzovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: He was the man who signed your release documents after 18 days?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He is the person who signed my release document after 18 days which I can provide as evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: In Trnopolje at this time as you were released yourself because of health reasons, is it right that other people were being released at this time as well?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At that time a bus was -- a bus load was released and there were three men among us and the rest were women who were going to go to Donja Puharska.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I have no further questions, thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Niemann?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Witness, the Red Cross that was at Trnopolje camp that you just mentioned, was that the local Red Cross or was it the International Red Cross or do you not know?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Excuse me for having to laugh! During my stay in the camp there was no presence of the International Red Cross. We had to call it the Red Cross because they wore, the people who, the personnel there wore the Red Cross. I do not know if it was blood or help, I could not tell you that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Thank you. Nothing further, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Kay?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Nothing arises, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Just one question, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Regarding your testimony about Trnopolje camp, you said that there was an area where persons could not enter without special permission. You said, as I recall, that was the area near the cafe and the first aid, I think you identified it as, that would be the ambulanta, I guess. Why is that so, and what do you mean by special permission?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can tell you that you needed special permission because there that part was used, this ambulanta -- just not to be misunderstood, it was just a cover for some help, because I was looking for medication but Pasic worked there, and this is what he told me, "I know that you are sick but I cannot give you, there is nothing that I can give you. I have a pill that I can give you just to soothe your pain, nothing else". This ambulanta existed so that when a person was well beaten up, that somebody would bandage him and so that he would not die that moment or some died, I do not know. So they were bandaged people -- they were bandaging people there when they were beaten that day.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: My question was really trying to focus on how you got into the area. We have seen photos of Trnopolje and we have a diagram that someone prepared, another witness. It is my understanding, at least, that you would have to pass a sentry post as you came into the road to Trnopolje, but that there was a fence around the environs of the camp itself. I would define "camp" as being that area where you had the commune. For example, there was a theatre there, formerly it was a theatre, a school, where the inmates were kept. There was, as I understand, a fence around that area, that the fence had been there before and it remained for a certain point in time. There were fences in certain other areas. But I am really focusing on the other side of the fence where there was a road that comes through and you come in, as I understand it, past a sentry post and across the road there is a bar, for example, and some other places that you described. You said that you needed special permission to be in that area. My question is, what do you mean by "special permission" and how do you know that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: An inmate who was across the gymnasium, there was an open space where it was not covered and down from there there was construction supplies store and warehouse and then that was enclosed, before the war where those construction supplies were sold, and that was separated from the Local Commune and the school house. Where you went upstairs to the Local Commune down off the dom Trnopolje, not the school house, of the dom building, in Trnopolje, where you went upstairs, up the stairs, an inmate who was above that line in the ground had to pass along that wall, one by one, so that he would be visible, so there would not be a crowd. Maybe they were afraid of crowds. So that path you could go to the ambulanta or the Red Cross and you go, 15, 20, 30 of you, and they say, "Stop, no more until these are done with their business", the business, what are you looking for? You are looking for a pass to go somewhere. You wanted medical aid, you want something from the Red Cross or you were looking for somebody. They were looking for a person they knew either in the Serb military or in Trnopolje or down in Babici or Kararici or whatever village, who were looking for their neighbours or whoever. At that time, during that period of time when I was there, it was still -- Trnopolje was still not fully cleansed of Muslims. Still in the area of Trnopolje around the camp there were civilians in their own houses. Kozarac had not been cleansed completely down Trnopolje. They were going village by village, hamlet by hamlet, and they were cleansing down towards Trnopolje. When they came to Kamicani, they went down and they went village by village, hamlet by hamlet. Maybe they could not get to it, I do not know what the plan was, I do not know, but there were still the Trnopolje people in their own houses, that mixture. Somebody may have been afraid, but this is my personal view. So 15, 20 or 30 of us had to go to this open space where I told you that you needed a special permission. You could not go whenever you wanted and in whichever way you wanted. You had to report and then, let us say, five of us and that is the special permission, so -----

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Yes, I understand. Did you need special permission to get past the sentry post on that road, or there were two roads, I guess, that you could take to leave this area. Did you need special permission? Would one need special permission to pass the sentry post?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Where we were and where I told you that I was, for that part of the camp you did not need a special permission, but outside of the gate, outside of the iron gate, for that you needed special permission. That means to get out on the road. For that you needed special permission, whereas within the perimeter you just need permission of the guards, so that you would not have 50, 100 people going. Only five, 10 were allowed to get in, so that they would finish their business. Sometimes they were just forbidden completely. You know, for instance, nobody was there in those offices so you could not go there or it was lunch time, so simply ----

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Really, we are talking about inmates when you said "special permission", is that not so?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: When did you arrive at Trnopolje?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I arrived in the Trnopolje camp nine days after which I spent in Keraterm.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: You were in Keraterm nine or 10 days?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Nine days.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Nine days?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Tenth day, on the tenth day, yes, on the tenth day, I was already in Trnopolje.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Then you stayed at Trnopolje 17 to 19 days?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I stayed in Trnopolje 18 to 19 days and I got a pass to go to Donja Puharska.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: You testified you saw Mr. Tadic at Trnopolje but when was that? How long after you had arrived at Trnopolje?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know. The data, the date I do not know. It is my opinion that it was the morning, that it was a Wednesday, but dates are so confused that I did not know who I was. I knew Dusan as a neighbour and I did not know many younger people, but I remember him as the first door neighbour, and maybe also he is in my memory also because, not Mr. Tadic, but his father, I remember him well.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: OK, thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: So through him I knew him as well.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Niemann, do you have additional questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: No, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Kay?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Nothing arises, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Is there any objection to the witness being permanently excused?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: No, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Sir, you are permanently excused. That means that you may leave. You, however, should remain in your seat until the Judges leave and then we will make the necessary arrangements so that you may leave. Thank you so much for coming. We will stand in recess for ----

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: A question, I am sorry, a request? Since you thanked me, I also want to thank the entire Tribunal, and I wish that the Tribunal fulfils everything that it has set out to do. I do not want to give pain to anybody, including this Dule, so I think that I have spoken the truth.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Thank you so. We will stand in recess for 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, will you call the next witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour, thank you. Before I call the next witness, I wanted to advise the Court (and also before the Court puts on its earphones) that the next speaker, although a native speaker of the Bosnian language, will be testifying in English, so his comprehension and speaking skills, although not flawless, are certainly sufficiently to permit him and probably enhance communication and, more importantly, I think, the effect of getting information simultaneously or in staggered form in two languages one understands is very, very difficult. So this is a preferable approach, I believe. The next witness is Emsud Velic. EMSUD VELIC, called.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Sir, would you take the oath that is being handed to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: You will put your, turn on the microphone there, please. You may be seated. Thank you, sir. We heard you.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Sir, what is your name?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Emsud Velic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: How old are you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: 24 years old.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Were you born in?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In a village called Kevljani.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Where is Kevljani located relative to the town of Kozarac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: About six kilometres.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Were you raised in Kevljani?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Are you a Bosnian Muslim?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Where did you go to school?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: First four years I went to the local school in Kevljani, next four years in Omarska and the last three years in Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: In March 1991, did you begin your basic military service with the JNA?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Velic, during the time you were growing up, how did the young men of the area, Muslims, Serbs and Croats, feel about the prospect of military service?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They felt very good. I mean, to be in the army at that time before the war, you know, it was like feeling you are very proud to go into the army. It is, you know, when you go to the army and you have your duty and everything, you felt when you came back you felt as you are, you know, grown up and that you are really a man afterwards. A lot of people, I mean, which could not go because either they were disabled or sick, you know, sometimes they felt lesser men than they are supposed to be.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: When you began your military service, where were you sent? Where did you serve?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They sent me in Slovenia in a town called Crnomelj.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Around the beginning of June were you assigned to guard an ammunition depot?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Was that right around the time of the beginning of the war in Slovenia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: After the conflict began, was your unit cut off by Slovenian troops?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: How long was your unit cut off in this fashion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: About five days or a week, something like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Did your unit finally surrender?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, we did.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: When you surrendered, how were you and the others treated by Slovenian troops?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We were treated very well. I mean, really, we did not know what to expect when we were going down to the road to meet them, but really they were friendly to all of us. They did not do any harm to us, nothing. They gave us food, drinks, everything. Then they took us to the town, gave us the phone to call the family and relatives that we are OK, you know, that they can come to pick us up, to go home and, you know, we were really treated very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Did they make any distinction between which soldiers were Muslim, Serb, Croat?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Did the Red Cross assist in arranging for members of your unit to return home?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, they did.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: After you returned home were you then ordered to report to the military barracks in Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: What assignment did you later receive?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Later on, maybe 20, 25 days after spending in Prijedor, they assigned me to the ammunition depot in a town called Ustikolina near Foca.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: When was your basic military service due to be completed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In March 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Did you leave the army before the completion of your basic service?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: When did you leave?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On December 21st 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Velic, why did you leave the service before the completion of your military obligation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, while I was there in Ustikolina a lot of things were going on. I mean, the war was already starting in Croatia. Then I was guarding the ammunition depot in that town. So almost every night we, you know, between eight or 10 trailers coming every night and we were loading them with the munition, grenades and all kinds of firearms, you know. When we were loading those trucks, I mean, the drivers or whoever told me that goes, it goes to Dubrovnik, at that time, Vukovar, and I really did not feel good being part of that, you know, because I know every case that I put in that truck is going either kill someone or destroy something. I really did not want to be any part of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Was there any expression of nationalistic sentiment in the army at that time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Who did you hear that from and what sorts of things were expressed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I heard most from reservists from Serbia and Montenegro who were coming to that base. It was just tough for them before they go to either Vukovar or Dubrovnik or wherever they are assigned to go and, you know, when they were coming, they were acting like they own everything there, you know. So they were starting telling, you know, how they, where they go, what they are going to do to destroy, to kill, to burn, to liberate Croatia and, you know, to make it part of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Was that sentiment and those expressions hidden or open?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Open. They felt very strong about it. I mean, they were not afraid of anything at that time because it was too many of them, you know, and its army, and they really felt army is there, so .....

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Were soldiers allowed to dress or wear their hair in different ways from the traditional army in order to express nationalistic identification?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, especially when the war started and especially somewhere around one month before I left the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: How was that? In what ways did they dress or look different from the typical army?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I mean, when you are in a typical army, you always have to be clean shaved every morning, hair cut, you know, like in the army, short, dress properly, you know, not to get loose, to put your shirt, you know, to put on your pants or something like that. No, you really have to be clean and tidy, like you have to give the example to other people how to be. At that time really they really did not care about that any more. They were just -- I mean, especially the Serbian soldiers, they really felt very, very free and very strong, especially when those reservists came, you know. So, really, they act like one of them. They wanted to be one of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Was there any particular look that some people adopted?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Excuse me?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Any particular style or look that some people adopted?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I mean, you know, sometimes when those reservists come there, either they are drunk, you know, and they would start singing those songs. They joined them in singing with them, you know, and then they would totally isolate us. You know, we were just separate from them. We did not -- we were allowed to go, you know, to be with them when you wanted to go there, but, you know, we were just isolated, you know, and keep quiet because you are afraid to say something if they, you know, even though at that time the war was not in Bosnia at that time, but still we were afraid, you know, to say who we were.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: When you say singing those songs, do you mean Serbian nationalist songs?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: After you left the army did you return to Kevljani?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Were you living at home with your family?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Were you doing work around the village?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Were you also going out a lot?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Where were you spending most of your time when you went out?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In Kozarac.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Velic, in the time before you went to the army did you know Dule Tadic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, not personally but just by seeing him and knowing who he is.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Even before you knew who he was, had you heard of him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Why had you heard of him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Because he was in -- he was in some kind of martial art competition, and you could hear of other people talking about him, specially when you go in Kozarac, even though at the time I did not met him personally. I mean, I did not know his face, but I could hear the stories he was good at those -- in those competition, you know, doing well and, sort of, he was some kind of local celebrity.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: How did you come to learn who he was and become familiar with his face?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When he opened a bar in Kozarac.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: After that bar was opened did you go there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Any particular reason?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, first, the first time just, you know, when something new opened, just you go there to check it out because it is new. You are interested. You want to see what is going on there, how is it, who is down there, you know.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: After you went there, did you become interested in meeting the owner or seeing the owner?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not really meeting him, but just to see who he is, you know, because I heard of him before. I never see him, you know, face to face.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: After you went to the bar did it increase your interest in seeing him face to face?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Why was that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I mean, because now he owns the bar so the bar, there is more chance for me to see him personally because I assumed -- I mean, he was the owner so he is going to be there, so that is the chance. I went in there. You know, there were some of my friends, and first time when I see him, I mean, I asked my friends whether they knew him, how he looked. You know, "Is that him?" or "Is that him?" until he did not show up and they told me, "That is him".

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Did you see anything in the bar which had anything to do with his martial arts success or that let people know who the owner of the bar was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: What was that or what sorts of things were those?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On the walls, on the shelves, there were trophies, medals, some kind of, you know, pictures of him fighting with someone in competition and some from newspapers, some articles.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: So did that increase the impression that he was a local celebrity whom you were interested in?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: For me, yes, I mean, not many people around there were, you know, known in other communities than their own, you know.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: All right. After the first time that you saw him in the bar, did you continue to see him in the bar on more occasions until the time you went to the army?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, almost every time when I went there before I went to the army, I saw him, you know, sometimes but I mean not all the time. You know, either he is going to be at the bar or walk out from the kitchen or when I was coming in, I always check everything who is in there because that is the kind of normal day, when you go into the restaurant or the bar, you first go through the restaurant or bar to check who is there, you know, because most of the time either of your friends, someone whom you knew. So if there is there someone, you will sit with them. Then I saw him in that small, separate portion of the bar sitting there with someone.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: So the bar had a small separated portion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: By the time you left to do your military service, were you familiar with who Dule Tadic was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: When you returned to the area after leaving the army and were going out to Kozarac a lot, did you continue to go to the bar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: What was the name of that bar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: "Nipon".

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Did you go there as often as you had before, less often or more often than in the past?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: More often than in the past.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: How often were you in the Nipon from the time you returned to Kevljani and the Kozarac area until the war broke out?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the Nipon I was on Saturdays, almost every Saturday there, spending there between an hour and two hours, sometimes two hours, sometimes one hour. But Saturdays almost every night, or on Wednesdays and Fridays, not exactly every Wednesday or Friday, but sometimes between half an hour and an hour.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Did Mr. Tadic continue to be around the bar doing the things that you described him doing before?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, he did.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Velic, let me direct your attention now to the beginning of the attack on the Kozarac area on May 24th. Where were you when the attack began?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In my village, that is my home.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: What was the reaction in Kevljani when the shelling began?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Chaos, panic, people running through the village. You know, women trying to find their children because, like in every village, they were playing that day, you know. We really did not expect that is going to happen. So, I mean, just total panic in the village.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Did you make any efforts to contact anyone outside the area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: What did you try to do?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was trying to reach one man in Prijedor, to ask him, you know, what is going on. Maybe they know better than us. But soon I pick up the phone.
